summary: Colly is a Go-native web scraping framework built around a callback-driven Collector abstraction. Users register OnHTML/OnXML/OnRequest/OnResponse/OnError callbacks on a Collector instance, then call Visit() to begin recursive crawling. The core is a single ~1,700-line file (colly.go) that orchestrates HTTP requests through a pluggable httpBackend with domain-based rate limiting (LimitRule uses buffered channels as semaphores), deduplication via fnv-hashed URL storage, robots.txt parsing, cookie/session management, proxy support, and optional disk caching with gob serialization. The queue package adds multi-threaded URL queue consumption, the storage package provides a swappable interface for visited-URL and cookie persistence. Verified from source: it does NOT include JavaScript rendering, structured data schemas, or built-in distributed backends — distributed support is DIY via the Storage interface.

findings.description: 1. Callback-based crawl lifecycle: OnRequest, OnRequestHeaders, OnResponseHeaders, OnResponse, OnHTML (CSS selector via goquery), OnXML (XPath via htmlquery/xmlquery), OnError, OnScraped. 2. Domain-based rate limiting with configurable parallelism and random delays (LimitRule with buffered channel semaphore). 3. URL deduplication via FNV-64 hash of canonical URL + (POST) body, stored in pluggable Storage interface. 4. robots.txt checking with caching per host (disabled by default, opt-in). 5. Pluggable storage backend (InMemoryStorage default, interface supports Redis/SQL implementations). 6. Request serialization to JSON for queue-based distributed processing. 7. Async goroutine for non-blocking crawls with WaitGroup coordination. 8. Disk-based GET request caching with gob encoding and SHA1-hashed filenames. 9. Proxy support (http/socks5). 10. Gzip decompression probing (checks magic bytes). 11. Character encoding detection (chardet). 12. Configurable max body size, max depth, max requests, domain allow/deny, URL regex filters. 13. Per-request Context map for passing data across the callback chain. 14. HTTP tracing for timing metrics.

apiSurface: Users create a Collector via colly.NewCollector() with optional functional options (e.g., colly.MaxDepth(2), colly.AllowedDomains("example.com")). They register callbacks: c.OnHTML("a[href]", fn), c.OnRequest(fn), c.OnResponse(fn), c.OnError(fn). Crawling starts with c.Visit(url) or r.Visit(url) from within a callback. Rate limiting: c.Limit(&colly.LimitRule{DomainGlob: "*", Parallelism: 2, Delay: 1*time.Second}). Structured data extraction happens in user code — push data into a struct, channel, or file. POST/HEAD/multipart support via c.Post(Post]). Queue: serializable Request objects are marshaled and stored; any Collector can unmarshal and process them, enabling decoupled/reprocessed-scaled architecture. Key extensibility points: SetStorage(Storage), SetProxy(proxyURL), WithTransport(http.RoundTrippers), SetCookieJar/jar), SetClient(http.Client).
integrationPoints: 1. Playwright/Selenium integration: Colly has no JS rendering — you could inject FETCH requests via Playwright's RequestInterceptor onto the network pipeline, or POST (hand-crafted, script-injected, page objects), or use scrapingbee/puppeteer to offline render URLs. The pipeline would feed. 2. Queue/RabbitMQ: transform each domain-pages results from Playwright into colly-style scraped bodies then serialized via Request.Marshal and posted to an external task/Rabbit system. The Storage interface supports any backend (proof: InMemoryStorage is just one impl; you could impl a SQLite or queue-backed storage that drops both visited hashes and cookies). 3. Structured extraction: colly cannot produce schematized laptop specs natively — it calls collymethodOnHTML/Bytes/Base/Datas for individual pages but you must write the (CSS/xpath per-page, Brand, Model, Price, etc) yourself. This is where custom extraction middleware (like Playwright + colly + LM) is uniquely possible. 4. 5. Match: colly has no fuzzy matching or entity resolution — the pipeline would own that. colly's visited hash storage could be used as a dedup both within single-prices-pages and between models (to avoid re-fetching the same URL). 5. Playwright integration via channels: an API call to a sidecar browser.x opens page, colly callback spits values to a custom iterator that feeds Playwright.
strengthsForVeridian: Excellent as a passive, high-throughput HTML fetch layer behind a Playwright browser for JS-rendered pages: the domain-based rate limiting, robots.txt checking, and caching would give good control over polite crawling. The Storage interface enables plugging in visited-URL persistence (Redis/MySQL) so multiple scraper processes can coordinate. The Request.Marshal/unmarshal pattern enables decoupled task distribution — you could pre-seed a Redis queue with serialized page URLs and let colly-based workers consume them. The callback model separates crawling concerns (politeness, dedup, fetching) from extraction concerns (parsing, DOM traversal) cleanly. Well-tested codebase (colly_test.go is ~55KB, comparable to core library) with concurrent safety (RW locks, atomic counters). Go’s memory model means no GC surprises under load.
weaknessesForVeridian: No JavaScript rendering — colly fetches raw HTML only; it cannot see content injected by React, Angular, client-side scripts, or AJAX. A separate headless browsing step is and must be bolted externally (Playwright or similar). No built-in extraction framework — there is no schematization, no Schema DSL, no transformation to output. Everything is write-once inline callback code. No RFC-style retry (backoff, idempotency tracking) — retry is only via r.Retry() which fires the same request statelessly. No SQS/Pub/Sub matrix integration — so the "distributed scraping" requires substantial plumbing work. The heavy single-author maintainer structure (Adam) is a bus-factor risk. The CHANGELOG/documentation gap means the README’s last known version is 2.1.0 (2020) but the code has ~6 years of un-documented changes — concepts of “gzip probing”, reworked visit limiting, etc. are invisible to the docs. Go-only — no Python bindings, no Go-Python interop in a Python-dominant project.
